strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: explaining black-box predictions through interpretable attributes while allowing omitted attributes to induce confounding. This has an identifiable audience in explainable AI, causal discovery, and model auditing.

Using PAGs is a principled choice under the stated causal assumptions. The background knowledge that predictions cannot cause image content is well motivated, and the framework can explicitly represent unresolved causal relationships.

The shape simulation makes the intended distinction between causal and confounded attributes concrete. The applications include bootstrap stability analyses and an alternative discovery algorithm, with substantive disagreements reported.

The manuscript generally communicates the framework clearly and discusses important limitations, including partial identifiability, annotation errors, and dependence on feature selection and domain knowledge.
weaknesses: Necessary: The X-ray sampling design undermines its causal interpretation. Section 6.1 selects 120 pneumonia images and 120 controls with 'no findings,' so inclusion depends on diagnosis and explanatory findings. This can introduce selection bias, whereas Section 3 dismisses selection as irrelevant and the subsequent interpretations assume its absence. Robustness to latent confounding does not resolve this problem. Account for the sampling mechanism or narrow this application to a descriptive illustration; clinical plausibility does not independently validate the inferred causes.

Necessary: The empirical conclusions exceed what the reported edge scores establish. Section 6.3 combines directed and partially directed edges, although a stable Zi o→ Yhat edge can remain entirely attributable to confounding. Conversely, absence of adjacency does not exclude a mediated causal effect. Consequently, the causal relevance and irrelevance claims in Figures 9–10 and Section 6.4 are too strong. Distinguish definite from possible ancestry, and restrict noncausality claims to exclusions supported by the full graph. Bootstrap frequency is not a probability of causation.

Necessary: Example 1 and Appendix A need a consistent intervention estimand and corrected derivation. Appendix A.2 retains the allegedly omitted Z3 as a fixed value in coalition calculations rather than deriving quantities from the available observations. Appendix A.1 leaves Z1's distribution unchanged when intervening on Z2, despite the stated Z2→Z1 relationship. These expressions are not generally macro-level interventional expectations under the supplied SCM. Clarify whether interventions act on causal attributes or copied model inputs, and demonstrate omitted-confounder bias without conflating it with changes to the attribution game.

Necessary: The reliability of the empirical conditional-independence tests needs further support. The bird analysis combines 26 categorical attributes with conditioning sets of up to four variables; the X-ray analysis has only 240 images and potentially sparse findings. Contingency-table diagnostics and handling of sparse tests are unreported. The sample and train/test splits actually used for discovery are also unclear. Bootstrap stability cannot correct systematic testing errors, and GRaSP-FCI changes the leading bird attributes substantially. Supply these details and targeted robustness evidence, or explicitly limit the findings to exploratory results.

Optional: A comparison using the same macro-level attributes with an associative or causally sufficient baseline would better isolate the benefit of allowing hidden confounding. The selected LIME/SHAP examples primarily establish a difference in explanatory granularity, rather than comparative causal accuracy. Complete analysis code and split specifications would also improve reproducibility.
